statement: How many three-digit numbers use only odd digits and never have two equal digits side by side? (For example, 535 counts but 553 does not.)

choices.misconception: I made all three digits different from each other, but the first and last digits are allowed to match.
I gave every place only four choices, including the first digit, which actually has all five odd digits available.
I took the 125 all-odd numbers and removed only the 5 with all three digits equal, missing numbers like 553.
I ignored the side-by-side rule and counted every number made of odd digits, which is 5 times 5 times 5.

hints: Fill the places one at a time, from left to right.
Use the multiplication principle, but let the restriction shape each count: a place only has to avoid the digit immediately before it, not every earlier digit.
The first digit has 5 odd choices. The second must differ from the first, and the third must differ only from the second.

solutions.reliable: Choose the hundreds digit from 1, 3, 5, 7, 9: 5 ways. The tens digit is odd but not equal to the hundreds digit: 4 ways. The units digit is odd but not equal to the tens digit: 4 ways, and it may equal the hundreds digit. Total 5 times 4 times 4, which is 80. The transferable idea: a restriction that only links neighbours costs one choice per place, so count place by place and ask exactly what each place must avoid.
solutions.elegant: Of the 125 all-odd numbers, those with the first two digits equal number 25 and those with the last two equal number 25, and 5 numbers do both. So 125 minus 25 minus 25 plus 5 is 80, matching the direct count.

whyOnTest: Restricted counting tests whether you read the restriction exactly: neighbours only, not all digits, which is the difference between 80 and 60.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
